Justice J.D. Kapoor (Oral)  

1. Since the respondent has appeared on his own and wants to argue on merits, appeal is being decided on merits.

2. On account of having sold highly defective car of Tata Indigo LS Diesel make, the appellant vide impugned order dated 25th July, 2007 has been directed to replace the defective vehicle and also to pay Rs. 25,000/- as compensation and Rs. 5000/- as cost of litigation.

3. Feeling aggrieved the appellant has preferred this appeal.

4. Relevant facts leading to impugned order in brief were that the respondent purchased a Tata Indigo LS Diesel Car on 29.6.2006 from M/s Sanya Automobiles Pvt. Ltd. , authorized dealer of M/s Tata Motors the appellant. According to him , appellant and respondent no. 2 passed on to him second hand car as new car and he learned about the deception when within half an hour the rear view mirror fell down and noise started coming from steering and shockers. He complained to appellant but he was assured they were minor problems and would be removed in first service. The problem, however, persisted and the respondent took the vehicle to M/s Indicare Motors , authorized service station of appellant but the problem could not be rectified. Further the vehicle was subjected to repeated repairs but without any results. The steering problem, continued despite inspection by the experts of the company, supplier of power steering to Tata Motors. The power steering was changed but the problem continued.

On 23.9.2006 the rack and pinion were also changed but the problem persisted. On 18.11.2006 steering column was changed but without any improvement in the functioning of the vehicle. On 8.1.2007 power steering and pumps were changed but the defect could not be rectified and the noise continued from the steering as well as from the shockers. Within six months of the purchase paint from the roof of the vehicle started peeling off which gave rise to the suspicion that it was an old car and had been passed off as new after repainting. Lastly the vehicle was taken to Sanya Motors. They carried out the trial on 15.1.2007 yet the defects could not be removed. The respondent approached everybody who mattered in the Tata Motors (names of some officials of appellant have been mentioned in the complaint) requesting them to replace the defective vehicle but to no avail.

5. In their defence, the appellant denied allegation that old car was passed on to the complainant as new one after repainting. According to respondent no. 1 there were some minor problems pointed by the respondent which were rectified to his satisfaction. Appellant admitted that there was peeling of the paint but according to it, it was on account of some acid having fallen on the paint and not on account of some defective paint used on the vehicle. While denying the allegations levelled by the respondent about the defects in the car, respondent no. 2 claimed that it was only a dealer and that liability, if any , was that of the manufacturer. Appellant has also denied that there was any manufacturing defect in the vehicle which was beyond rectification and that the minor problems pointed out by the respondent were attended to and the defects were rectified.

6. The impugned order has been assailed mainly on the premise that the respondent had failed to adduce expert evidence that there was manufacturing defect in the vehicle which was beyond rectification and further that the vehicle should have been sent for expert opinion under the provision of section 13(1)(c ) of the C.P. Act, 1986 before declaring manufacturing defects. There is no such provision under the law as it is the duty of the manufacturer to maintain the quality and standard of the vehicle. Section 13 (1)(c) does not apply as the expert opinion is obtained in case where samples of goods are taken for analysis . Section 13(I) (c) provides as under:

(c) where the complaint alleges a defect in the goods which cannot be determined without proper analysis or test of the goods, the District Forum shall obtain a sample of the goods from the complainant, seal it and authenticate it in the manner prescribed and refer the sample so sealed to the appropriate laboratory along with a direction that such laboratory make an analysis or test, whichever may be necessary, with a view to finding out whether such goods suffers from any defect alleged in the complaint or from any other defect and to report its findings thereon to the District Forum within a period of forty-five days of the receipt of the reference or within such extended period as may be granted by the District Forum

7. In our view, onus shifts to the manufactures to prove that the vehicle did not suffer from any defect including the manufacturing defect once the consumer proves from job cards that the vehicle was taken on large number of occasion for removing one defect or the other.

8. Every good or vehicle has to pass the test of its quality and standard on the touchstone of definition of word defect which in terms of section 2(I)(f) means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods. In such an eventuality there are four options open to the Consumer Forum. First to direct the trader to remove the defect, second is to replace the goods with new good with same standard and specification free from defect, third is to refund the price to the consumer charged by the trader, and fourth is to pay an amount as compensation for any loss injury suffered by the consumer due to negligence of the OP.

9. It is too much to expect from the consumer to get the services of an expert to prove the manufacturing defect as he has already suffered due to sale of defective vehicle and to ask him to pay further for engaging the services of the expert is too much to ask. Thus onus is heavily upon the manufacturer to prove that vehicle does not suffer from any manufacturing defect.

10. Even otherwise it is misconceived notion that goods purchased by the consumer cannot be replaced or the price thereof cannot be refunded unless and until the manufacturing defect is brought beyond the warranty period. The concept of warranty is that dealer is entitled to charge from the consumer for the repairs and if the defects in the goods continue during the warranty period or after the period of warranty for years together the goods have to be declared defective goods as conceptualized by section 2(1)(f) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 as detailed above.

11. In such type of cases we have taken a view that cost of the goods should be refunded so as to end the dispute once for all as replacement of any defective goods by new goods is not a solution as such replacement of the goods may not be upto the satisfaction of the consumer and this may relegate the parties to a second bout of litigation.

12. In the result, we partly allow the appeal by modifying the impugned order to the extent that instead of replacing the defective vehicle appellant shall refund the cost of the vehicle on the return of the vehicle after completing the formalities of transfer of registration certificate in the name of the appellant. Rest of the order is maintained.

13. F.D.R./ Bank Guarantee, if any, furnished by the appellant be returned forthwith after completion of due formalities.

14. A copy of this order as per statutory requirements, be forwarded to the parties free of charge and also to the concerned District Forum and thereafter the file be consigned to the record room.

15. Copy be sent to Presidents of all the District Forum.

Announced on the 17th December, 2008.
